name: Nickel-metal hydride
electrolyte: Potassium hydroxide-based alkaline solution (20 to 40% by weight)
self_discharge: Standard cells retain about 50 to 80% of capacity after 12 months (Energizer); low self-discharge cells about 70 to 85% after one year at 20 °C (Wikipedia)
summary: Nickel-metal hydride cells pair a nickel oxyhydroxide positive electrode with a hydrogen-absorbing alloy negative in an alkaline electrolyte, giving 1.2 V on a flat discharge curve. They are the common rechargeable AA and AAA cell and replaced nickel-cadmium in most consumer uses.
body:
## How it works

Energizer describes nickel-metal hydride as an extension of sealed nickel-cadmium technology with the cadmium negative electrode replaced by a hydrogen-absorbing metal alloy. On charge, the alloy takes up hydrogen from the water in the electrolyte (Alloy + H2O + e⁻ → Alloy(H) + OH⁻) and nickel hydroxide at the positive electrode is oxidized; on discharge, the alloy releases the hydrogen and nickel oxyhydroxide is reduced back to nickel hydroxide. The electrolyte is a 20 to 40% by weight alkaline hydroxide solution, the separator is usually a non-woven polyolefin, and each cell has a resealable safety vent. Energizer states that the metal hydride electrode has a theoretical capacity more than 40% higher than a cadmium electrode, giving energy densities more than 20% higher than an equivalent nickel-cadmium cell.

## Discharge behavior

After charge the open-circuit voltage is about 1.4 V; under load it drops quickly to a flat plateau near 1.2 V. Energizer rates its cells at 1.25 V, while IEC and Energizer's characteristics table use 1.2 V. The usual discharge cutoff is 0.9 V per cell, 75% of the 1.2 V midpoint, though at high drain rates (1 to 4 C) that cutoff can leave capacity unused. Driving cells in a series pack into reverse can shorten their life, so Energizer recommends removing the load before total discharge. Charge and discharge are rated from 0 to 50 °C, and storage from −20 to 30 °C.

Energizer recommends a standard charge of 0.1 C for 12 to 14 hours and a maintenance (trickle) charge below 0.025 C (C/40). It gives cycle life as several hundred cycles and a typical service life of 2 to 5 years. Standard cells retain about 50 to 80% of capacity after 12 months of storage. Memory effect, the voltage depression of about 150 mV seen in routinely part-discharged nickel-cadmium cells, is described by Energizer as no longer a concern with NiMH.

## Uses

NiMH is sold in the common round sizes as rechargeable replacements for primary cells, designated HR in IEC 61951-2 (HR6 for AA). Energizer positions it for devices that would otherwise need frequent battery replacement. Battery University also lists medical instruments, hybrid cars and industrial applications.

## History

Work on NiMH began at the Battelle-Geneva Research Center following the technology's invention in 1967. Research at Philips Laboratories and France's CNRS developed rare-earth hydride alloys for the negative electrode, and in 1987 Willems and Buschow demonstrated a successful cell based on them. The first consumer NiMH cells went on sale in 1989. In 2005, Sanyo introduced low self-discharge cells under the Eneloop name; manufacturers claim they retain 70 to 85% of capacity after a year at 20 °C, compared with about half for standard NiMH.

## Status

Current. IEC uses the letter H for nickel-metal hydride.
strengths: More than 20% higher energy density than nickel-cadmium (Energizer)
No cadmium; memory effect not a concern (Energizer)
Can outperform alkaline in high-drain devices
limitations: 1.2 V, lower than the 1.5 V of primary cells
Standard cells lose a large share of charge in storage
Cycle life of several hundred cycles (Energizer)
Charge and discharge limited to 0 to 50 °C
safety: Over-discharge of a series pack can drive cells into reverse polarity
Gases formed in overcharge are normally recombined inside the cell; a resealable safety vent relieves excess pressure
